name: Maximum Drawdown from a Price Series
description: Gives the largest percentage fall from a running peak to a later trough.
notes: Here the worst fall is from 120 to 90, 25 %. A key measure of downside risk for funds and trading systems.

name: Current Drawdown
description: Gives how far the latest value is below the highest value reached so far.
notes: Here 126 against a peak of 140 is a 10 % drawdown.

name: Calmar Ratio
description: Divides the annualised return by the maximum drawdown (usually over three years).
notes: Higher is better; values above 1 are considered good for hedge funds.

name: Sharpe Ratio from a Return Series
description: Computes the Sharpe ratio from a list of periodic returns: mean excess return divided by the sample standard deviation.
notes: Multiply by √(periods per year) to annualise (√12 for monthly data).

name: Sortino Ratio from a Return Series
expression: (mean(rs) - tgt) / sqrt(sum(k, 1, len(rs), min(at(rs, k) - tgt, 0)^2) / len(rs))
description: Divides the mean excess over a target by the downside deviation, which counts only returns below the target.
notes: Unlike Sharpe, upside volatility is not penalised.

name: Omega Ratio
expression: sum(if(rs > tgt, rs - tgt, 0)) / sum(if(rs < tgt, tgt - rs, 0))
description: Divides the total gains above a threshold by the total losses below it, using the whole return distribution.
notes: Values above 1 mean more gain than loss relative to the threshold.

name: Annualised Volatility from Periodic Returns
description: Scales the standard deviation of periodic returns to a yearly figure with the square-root-of-time rule.
notes: Use 252 for daily trading returns, 52 for weekly, 12 for monthly.

name: Historical Volatility from Prices
description: Computes annualised volatility from a price series through the standard deviation of log returns.
notes: This is the realised volatility that option traders compare with implied volatility.

name: Geometric Mean Return of a Series
description: Gives the constant per-period return that compounds to the same end value as the actual returns.
notes: Always at or below the arithmetic mean; approximately mean − variance/2.

name: Cumulative Return of a Series
description: Chains a list of periodic returns into the total return over the whole span.
notes: Returns compound: +10 % then −10 % is −1 %, not zero.

name: Volatility Drag (Geometric vs Arithmetic Return)
description: Approximates the compound (geometric) growth rate from the average return and volatility.
notes: A portfolio averaging 8 % with 20 % volatility compounds at only about 6 %.

name: Beta from Return Series
description: Estimates beta as the least-squares slope of asset returns against market returns (equal to cov/var).
notes: Use at least 36 monthly observations in practice.

name: Alpha from Return Series (Regression Intercept)
description: Estimates per-period alpha as the intercept of the regression of excess asset returns on excess market returns.
notes: Positive alpha means return beyond what the market exposure explains.

name: Tracking Error
description: Gives the standard deviation of the differences between portfolio and benchmark returns.
notes: Index funds aim for tracking errors of a few basis points; active funds often run 2–6 % a year.

name: Information Ratio from Return Series
description: Divides the average active return by the tracking error, measuring how consistently a manager beats the benchmark.
notes: Annualise by multiplying by √(periods per year).

name: Upside Capture Ratio
description: Compares the fund's returns with the benchmark's over the periods when the benchmark rose (simple-sum version).
notes: Above 100 % means the fund gained more than the market in up periods.

name: Downside Capture Ratio
description: Compares the fund's returns with the benchmark's over the periods when the benchmark fell.
notes: Below 100 % means the fund lost less than the market in down periods.

name: Modigliani Risk-Adjusted Performance (M²)
description: Rescales the portfolio to the market's volatility and reports the return it would then earn, so it can be compared directly with the market return.
notes: Ranks portfolios exactly as the Sharpe ratio does, but in percentage points.

name: Two-Asset Portfolio Volatility
description: Gives the volatility of a two-asset portfolio with weights w and 1 − w.
notes: Unless ρ = 1 it is below the weighted average of the two volatilities: the benefit of diversification.

name: Portfolio Volatility from a Covariance Matrix
description: Computes √(wᵀΣw), the volatility of a portfolio of any number of assets from its weights and covariance matrix.
notes: The covariance entries are ρᵢⱼσᵢσⱼ; the diagonal holds the variances.

name: Portfolio Expected Return
description: Weights each asset's expected return by its share of the portfolio.
notes: Weights should add up to 1 (negative weights are short positions).

name: Minimum-Variance Weight (Two Assets)
description: Gives the weight of asset 1 in the two-asset portfolio with the lowest possible volatility.
notes: With these inputs about 10.5 % goes to the riskier asset.

name: Tangency Portfolio Weight (Two Assets)
description: Gives the weight of asset 1 in the portfolio with the highest Sharpe ratio (the tangency portfolio on the efficient frontier).
notes: Combining this portfolio with cash gives the capital market line.

name: Inverse-Volatility (Risk Parity) Weight, Two Assets
description: Weights two assets in inverse proportion to their volatilities, so that (ignoring correlation) they contribute equal risk.
notes: A 20 %-volatility stock fund and a 5 % bond fund get 20 % and 80 %.

name: Diversification Ratio
description: Divides the weighted average of individual volatilities by the portfolio volatility (Choueifaty 2008).
notes: Equal to 1 with perfect correlation; the higher, the more diversification.

name: Mean–Variance Utility
description: Gives the certainty-equivalent return U = E(r) − ½Aσ² used to rank portfolios for an investor with risk aversion A.
notes: With A = 4 a portfolio of 8 % and 20 % volatility is worth the same as a sure 0 %.

name: Optimal Risky Share (Merton)

variables.label: Expected return of the risky asset

description: Gives the share of wealth to hold in the risky asset for an investor with constant relative risk aversion (Merton 1969).
notes: Values above 1 mean borrowing to invest.

name: Historical Value at Risk
description: Reads the loss not exceeded with the given confidence straight from the historical return distribution (interpolated percentile).
notes: Needs many observations; with few data points the tail is poorly estimated.

name: Expected Shortfall (Parametric, Normal)
description: Gives the average loss in the worst (1 − c) share of outcomes for normally distributed returns — the Basel III market-risk measure at 97.5 %.
notes: Always larger than VaR at the same confidence.

name: Expected Shortfall (Historical)
expression: -sum(if(rs <= percentile(rs, 1 - cl), rs, 0)) / sum(rs <= percentile(rs, 1 - cl)) * v
description: Averages the historical returns at or below the VaR threshold and turns the result into a money loss.
notes: Also called conditional VaR (CVaR).

name: Scaling VaR over a Horizon
description: Scales a one-day VaR to h days with the square-root-of-time rule, as in the Basel 10-day VaR.
notes: Valid only if daily returns are independent with the same distribution.

name: Probability of a Loss (Normal Returns)
description: Gives the chance that a normally distributed return is negative.
notes: With 7 % expected return and 15 % volatility there is about a 32 % chance of losing money in a year.

name: Probability of Loss over n Years
description: Gives the chance that the average yearly return over n years is negative, assuming independent normal returns.
notes: Falls from about 32 % over one year to 7 % over ten years in this example.

name: Gain Needed to Recover a Loss
description: Gives the percentage gain needed to get back to the starting value after a loss.
notes: A 50 % loss needs a 100 % gain to recover.

name: Arbitrage Pricing Theory Expected Return (Two Factors)
description: Gives the expected return under Ross's arbitrage pricing theory: the risk-free rate plus each factor exposure times its premium.
notes: Factors can be macroeconomic (inflation, industrial production) or statistical.

name: Fama–French Three-Factor Expected Return
expression: rf + bm * mrp + bs * smb + bh * hml
description: Adds size (small minus big) and value (high minus low book-to-market) premiums to the CAPM (Fama and French 1993).
notes: The five-factor version adds profitability (RMW) and investment (CMA).

name: Levered Beta (Hamada)
description: Converts an unlevered (asset) beta to the equity beta at a given debt-to-equity ratio.
notes: Used to take a peer group's beta and apply it to a company with a different capital structure.

name: Unlevered Beta (Hamada)
description: Removes the effect of debt from an equity beta to get the beta of the business itself.
notes: Assumes debt carries no market risk (debt beta zero).

name: Dollar-Cost Averaging Average Cost
description: Gives the average cost per share when the same amount is invested at each price: the harmonic mean of the prices.
notes: Always at or below the simple average price, because more shares are bought when prices are low.

name: Value After Regular Contributions and Growth (List of Returns)
expression: sum(k, 1, len(rs), pmt * prod(j, k, len(rs), 1 + at(rs, j)))

variables.label: Contribution at the start of each period

description: Grows a fixed contribution made at the start of each period through the actual sequence of returns.
notes: Unlike a lump sum, the order of returns matters when money is added over time (sequence risk).

name: Kelly Fraction for a Two-Outcome Bet with Loss Fraction
description: Gives the Kelly fraction when a win gains b and a loss loses a of the stake: f* = p/a − (1 − p)/b.
notes: Reduces to the classic (bp − q)/b when the whole stake is lost (a = 1).
